A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DIsoN research and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The retained method and matched experiments support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original OOD detection experiments across four medical imaging benchmarks, together with ablations and qualitative isolation results.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical evaluation and reports revised benchmark results, class-prediction robustness experiments, classifier accuracies, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same isolation objective, convergence score, decentralized updates, and class-conditional sampling. Clarified oversampling notation and newly discussed fine-tuning alternatives do not change the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same dermatology, chest X-ray, ultrasound, and histopathology coverage, including the same MIDOG domains and CCAgT/FNAC far-OOD tasks. The added class-prediction controls reuse these datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparators remain MSP, MDS, fDBD, ViM, iForest, CIDER, and PALM. The new runtime comparison reuses existing baselines, while the newly cited few-shot federated methods are discussed without being evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled evaluations assigning incorrect classes to all targets, only ID targets, or only OOD targets, plus partial fine-tuning and runtime evaluations. Appendix G specifically lowers Dermatology's maximum rounds from 300 to 150 for additional runtime experiments. The original benchmark splits, metrics, and main training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 3b and Appendix E add substantial analysis of dependence on predicted-class accuracy, including primary-model accuracies in Table 7. Appendix D reports worse performance with partial fine-tuning, and Appendices G–H expand runtime analysis. Existing augmentation, network-size, aggregation-weight, and PCA analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports benchmark point estimates without specifying repeated runs or seed variability. v2 reports three-seed means and standard deviations in Tables 1 and 13–14, explains variability of seed-wise macro averages, and adds runtime quantiles. This establishes new uncertainty reporting; v1's unspecified run count prevents inferring a particular increase in runs.

E6.justification: Many benchmark scores change under the newly specified three-seed aggregation. Table 1's CC-DIsoN average AUROC/FPR95 changes from 79.49/56.17 to 80.00/59.20. In Table 2, PALM's former far-OOD lead becomes a reported average AUROC tie at 98.3, with CC-DIsoN achieving lower FPR95, 4.4 versus 11.6. Class-error, classifier-accuracy, and detailed runtime results are also added.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1, Proposition 3.1, its assumptions, and the full Appendix B proof retain the same mathematical content. Distinguishing isolation labels from class labels and explicitly writing replicated target samples clarify existing notation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: isolation-based OOD scoring, decentralized comparison through parameter exchange, and class-conditioning. The claimed application scope and central performance claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of sensitivity to incorrect class predictions, limitations of frozen features, and robustness across aggregation weights. It expands the existing inference-cost caveat into discussion of asynchronous clinical workflows, parallel execution, and network latency. Some new robustness interpretations overgeneralize the mixed outcomes in Table 3b.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promised-code placeholder with a concrete repository link, explains the fixed convergence parameters, and discloses execution of eight concurrent instances on a 24 GB RTX A5000. It removes v1's per-dataset total GPU-hour estimates. Existing architecture and training-hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 newly distinguishes DIsoN from few-shot federated learning, citing FedAffect and Federated Few-Shot Learning. Additional references support discussion of imaging baselines, convergence thresholds, and clinical turnaround times. The original positioning relative to isolation forests and OOD detection remains intact.

P1.justification: Localized edits polish the introduction and clarify labels, oversampling, and centralized versus decentralized operation. Author affiliations and contribution/venue footnotes change, and new appendix sections organize the additional analyses. Most existing prose and the main section structure are retained.

P2.justification: The tabular presentation expands substantially: Table 3 gains a misclassification panel, Tables 1–2 change metric ordering and statistical presentation, and Tables 7–14 add accuracy, runtime, and uncertainty displays. Figures 1–7 retain their visual content, with several relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by supplying uncertainty across three seeds for the main benchmarks, testing dependence on class predictions, and quantifying runtime tradeoffs. These address important evidence gaps in v1. The code link also improves reproducibility information. Some new robustness prose overreaches—Table 3b reports ultrasound AUROC of 34.6 when ID classes are wrong—but this localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny.
